name: OpenTelemetry
summary: The vendor-neutral standard for producing and shipping traces, metrics and logs, with SDKs for most languages and a Collector to route the data.
intro: OpenTelemetry (OTel) is not a backend: it stores nothing and draws no dashboards. It is the plumbing in front of one. Language SDKs and auto-instrumentation libraries create spans, metrics and log records inside your code, named according to shared semantic conventions (`http.request.method`, `db.system.name`), and send them over OTLP, its wire protocol for gRPC and HTTP.

The OpenTelemetry Collector is a separate process that sits between your apps and your backends. Each pipeline chains receivers (OTLP, Prometheus scraping, Kafka and more), processors (batching, filtering, adding Kubernetes pod labels) and exporters (Prometheus, a tracing backend, a commercial vendor). Because the instrumentation is standard, switching backend means changing the Collector’s config, not re-instrumenting every service. OTel was formed in 2019 by merging OpenTracing and OpenCensus, and became a CNCF graduated project in May 2026.
strengths: Instrument once and switch backends freely; many vendors, and Prometheus itself, accept OTLP directly
One SDK and one set of conventions for traces, metrics and logs, so a log line can carry the trace ID of its request
The Collector can batch, sample, redact and fan out telemetry without touching application code
Auto-instrumentation for common frameworks in Java, Python, .NET, JavaScript and others gives traces with little or no code
limits: Maturity varies by language and signal: traces and metrics are stable in most SDKs, logs are still in development in several, and profiles are early
You still need somewhere to store and query the data; OTel only produces and moves it
The Collector has a long list of components and a large config surface; many contrib components are beta or alpha
Component names change between Collector releases (for example `otlphttp` is now `otlp_http`), so upgrades need care

snippet.title: A Collector that receives OTLP and pushes metrics to Prometheus

story: Google’s 2010 Dapper paper showed how to follow a single request across thousands of machines. In the years after, tracing and monitoring vendors each shipped their own agents and libraries, so instrumenting code meant committing to one vendor, and open-source libraries had no neutral way to add tracing. Two projects set out to fix that. OpenTracing, co-created by Dapper co-author Ben Sigelman, joined the CNCF in October 2016 as a vendor-neutral tracing API. In January 2018 Google open-sourced OpenCensus, a version of its internal Census library that collected both traces and metrics.

They solved the same problem in incompatible ways. As Sigelman and Google’s Morgan McLean wrote: “The biggest problem with either project has been the fact that there were two of them.” In May 2019 the two announced they were merging into OpenTelemetry, a new CNCF sandbox project with governance from Google, LightStep, Microsoft and Uber, and bridges so existing OpenTracing and OpenCensus code would keep working.

Logs joined traces and metrics, its OTLP protocol became a common wire format, and many observability vendors, and Prometheus itself, now accept it directly. OpenTelemetry became the CNCF’s highest-velocity project after Kubernetes and graduated in May 2026.

choices.choice: Separate the API from the SDK
choices.why: Libraries and frameworks depend only on the small API, which does nothing if no SDK is installed. The application owner then picks the SDK and exporters, so instrumented libraries never force a vendor on anyone.

Storage and visualisation are deliberately left to other tools. The project describes the goal plainly: you own the data you generate, with no vendor lock-in, so you can change backends without re-instrumenting your code.
Rather than start a third standard, the founders combined the two existing ones and promised software bridges, so code already written against either API could move over gradually.

timeline.text: Google publishes the Dapper paper on distributed tracing
OpenTracing joins the CNCF in October
OpenTracing and OpenCensus merge into OpenTelemetry, a CNCF sandbox project
Moves to CNCF incubation in August
Graduates from the CNCF in May
